Approximately 2,145 trees expected to be felled

The project is currently being undertaken by a joint venture of "China State Construction Hong Kong", "Airmine Construction", and "China State Construction Civil Engineering". According to a 2024 Legislative Council document, there are approximately 2,270 trees within the project scope, of which around 2,145 are expected to be felled, including 10 trees of "special value"—the Aquilaria sinensis (土沉香) and 2 Ormosia pachycarpa (茸莢紅豆). The authorities plan to replant approximately 2,140 trees upon completion, including Koelreuteria bipinnata (複羽葉�樹), Magnolia grandiflora (荷花玉蘭), and Michelia champaca (黃蘭), among others.

No shade from large trees — Residents: Heat feels even more intense in hot weather

Reporters recently surveyed the area from Claret Villa to Sai Kung Town Centre, finding that trees have been removed along several road sections, including Pak Wai, Claret Villa, Pak Sha Wan, Pak Kong, and the section leading to Sai Kung Town Centre. Tree felling is particularly noticeable in the Pak Kong area. Due to site formation works, reporters observed that nearly one-third of the trees on the hillside have been cut down; along the village road at Tai Chung Hau, at least 15 consecutive trees have also been felled. Some village residents said that with the reduction of roadside greenery along the way, the heat feels even more intense during hot weather.

Site formation works are being carried out on the Pak Kong hillside, where trees have been felled.

A hole was drilled into one of the felled large trees, and a bottle of orange juice was placed inside.

Approximately 1,900 trees inevitably need to be removed

In response to Jodi Media (《集誌社》) enquiries, the Highways Department stated that, because the relevant works run very close to vegetation-covered slopes on both sides of the road, some trees situated primarily on the slopes need to be removed or transplanted to free up sufficient space for the works. After survey, approximately 1,900 trees still inevitably need to be removed.

11 of 13 Aquilaria sinensis trees expected to be felled

The authorities stated that there are 13 Aquilaria sinensis trees within the project scope. Of these, 11 were assessed as unsuitable for transplantation due to their form, structure, and growing location and thus must be removed, while the remaining 2 are preserved in situ. Additionally, one Ormosia pachycarpa was assessed as likewise unsuitable for transplantation and must be removed; one camphor tree (樟樹) originally earmarked for transplantation was also assessed as needing removal. Three Indian figs (印度榕) are preserved in situ.

The authorities stated that the project team will plant approximately 2,000 trees at suitable locations within Sai Kung District, such as roadside greening zones, to enhance the landscape along the route and the Sai Kung community environment.

Aquilaria sinensis classified as Vulnerable

Aquilaria sinensis (土沉香) is a native Hong Kong tree species, mainly distributed in Sai Kung, the northeastern New Territories, and Lantau Island. As of 2021, there were approximately 5,000 mature Aquilaria sinensis trees in Hong Kong. The species is classified as rare and is listed as a protected plant under the Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance, and as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Because its resin can be refined into the precious fragrance "agarwood" (沉香), in earlier years—particularly in the Sai Kung area—mainland "tree-cutting gangs" illegally came to Hong Kong to fell the trees, with black-market prices exceeding ten thousand Hong Kong dollars.

As for Ormosia pachycarpa (茸莢紅豆), it is an evergreen tree of the Fabaceae family Ormosia genus, classified by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department as a rare and precious plant. The species was first discovered in Happy Valley in 1850 and is now considered endangered within China.

Pak Wai Village resident Regina purchased a village house some years ago. A self-described "flower fanatic," she decided to buy the house entirely because there was an old tree in front of it, which she laughingly likened to a "treasure." Upon learning of tree-felling in the surrounding area, she said emotionally: "It's 2,000 trees, not 200!" She believes Sai Kung has long enjoyed the reputation of being "Hong Kong's back garden" and questioned, "Without 2,000 trees, can Sai Kung still be considered Hong Kong's back garden?"

Regina, who calls herself a "flower fanatic," originally decided to buy her home in Sai Kung entirely because of the old tree in front of the house, which she described as finding a "treasure." (Photo provided by Regina)

She said trees are living things that may take a hundred years to grow; once lost, they are hard to restore, including the precious Aquilaria sinensis. Taking Pak Wai Village as an example, she noted that visitors may not remember the village name but do remember an old tree at the village entrance, which has even become a landmark for the bus stop. "I can see the mountain precisely because of these trees—try without them, how would I see the mountain?" She believes the Government should not take a one-size-fits-all approach at the expense of nature conservation.

Neighbours have deep affection for old trees

Another Sai Kung resident, Amy, said that three generations of her family, including her children, have grown up in Sai Kung. "Seeing the trees gone is like all those years of growing up gone too." Not wearing glasses, she joked that over the years her eyesight has been excellent precisely because she has been surrounded by greenery, with lush woodland in the distance. "Suddenly they cut the trees down, and even the children are going to become nearsighted."

Beyond witnessing the disappearance of trees, she lamented the changes Sai Kung has undergone over the years—for example, several historic buildings off the Sai Kung highway, including the 1946-established "China Paint" (中華製漆) paint factory, with its "Chrysanthemum," "Giraffe," and "Toy" brand logos, will be demolished and redeveloped into housing. She also cited how a recent super typhoon brought down an old tree in the town, attracting neighbours to take photos—reflecting the deep affection residents have for old trees.

Roadside scenery along the highway has become "scruffy and dilapidated"

Sai Kung resident Mr. Tam said that, although he does not know the exact number of trees felled, the reduction of trees along the route is clearly visible. "There used to be so many trees, it was comfortable. Now you see it all scruffy and dilapidated, it feels uncomfortable." He noted that when he moved to Sai Kung one to two years ago, large-scale tree felling had not yet begun; he also felt it was a pity that the Aquilaria sinensis were being cut down. He questioned whether widening the road would ease congestion, noting that going into Sai Kung on holidays is "expected to be jammed."

An 84-year-old Sai Kung resident, "Uncle," has lived in the area for more than 20 years. He said that since over a thousand trees were felled, the Sai Kung landscape has become unrecognisable, and he questioned, "What do traffic jams have to do with those trees? Your cars don't pass through the trees, do they?"

Friends of the Earth (地球之友) director Wong Cheuk-yuet said that when engineering consultants assess trees, though it may not be intentional, for the convenience of construction there is often a tendency to "pick bones out of eggs"—meaning, if it cannot be moved, it is simply felled—rather than making every effort to save each tree. For example, trees of ordinary species must be nearly "perfect" to be retained; even when trees are in fair condition, if they have minor defects or slightly poorer growing space, the report will list adverse factors. Large trees may cost over a million dollars to transplant, or may decline during the process or while a suitable site is being found.

Aquilaria sinensis should in principle be preserved as far as possible

He acknowledged that some Sai Kung locations are on slopes, where digging root balls and transplanting is more difficult, but if conservation is the goal, measures such as substantial crown pruning and reducing root ball size should be considered, with "keeping the species alive" as the primary objective. With the significant decline in Aquilaria sinensis numbers, the principle should be to preserve them as far as possible. He also expressed concern that, as the road gains additional traffic lanes and dividing facilities, there will be a lack of planting space along the route, transforming the formerly tree-shaded surroundings into vast expanses of concrete, which in the long run may affect the experience of waiting for and walking along the road.
